title: Devin.ai is doing 80% of Rivo's Engineering Work
speakers_and_attribution: Stuart is the principal guest demonstrating Rivo's engineering workflows; his first name is confirmed in conversation, while the company identification also relies on the title and a spoken reference captioned as Revo. Adam Robinson participates alongside Rob and at least one technical participant whose identity is not securely established. The technical participant refers to Adam in the third person and must not be treated as Adam. Adam's strongest attributable material concerns RB2B, free users, distribution, staffing and his planned return to customer contact near the end. Earlier Adam attributions are contextual and marked accordingly. Captions are automatic and not diarized; names and product spellings vary.
summary: Stuart demonstrates Rivo's effort to make AI agents responsible for most implementation work through codebase cleanup, explicit documentation, standardized prompts, automated testing and layered AI review. The spoken 80% figure is an operating goal and workflow model, not a verified share of all engineering work. He describes successful integration and help-document workflows, while acknowledging preparation costs and stronger results on familiar, repeatable tasks than novel work. The discussion also covers developer adoption, ticket quality, Shopify distribution changes and moving upmarket. In the final minutes, Adam questions the value of RB2B's free tier, explains limits to its agency-driven content opportunity, reports two departures and states a goal of reaching 10 million with three named people. He plans to spend six months writing LinkedIn posts, answering support tickets and talking to customers after recognizing that he had become disconnected from them.

key_learnings.claim: Stuart uses AI code review to identify small defects without making a human colleague repeatedly deliver uncomfortable criticism; review summaries also make pull requests easier to assess.
key_learnings.speaker: Stuart
key_learnings.caveat: Guest's account of team dynamics and tool usefulness, not evidence about Adam's engineering organization.

key_learnings.claim: Rivo layers a lightweight review tool with a more comprehensive Claude review, using automated review as an accessible starting point for skeptical developers.
key_learnings.speaker: Stuart
key_learnings.caveat: The lightweight tool is inconsistently captioned as ellipsus, Ellipse and Eclipse. Claude was a recent addition; Stuart is uncertain about its configuration options.

key_learnings.claim: Stuart's intended operating model assigns humans the initial specification and final review, with an agent handling most implementation and AI performing an initial review pass.
key_learnings.speaker: Stuart
key_learnings.caveat: The 10/80/10 allocation is a proposed workflow model. Stuart explicitly describes moving toward 80% agent-written code, rather than reporting a measured company-wide result.

key_learnings.claim: Agent adoption required rebuilding the working environment and changing the codebase and development process; Stuart rejects the expectation that enabling the tool alone should produce reliable results.
key_learnings.speaker: Stuart
key_learnings.caveat: The short workspace setup and the multi-month organizational preparation are different activities. These are Rivo's reported costs, not universal requirements.

key_learnings.claim: Rivo reduced unused code, improved descriptive file names and documented established patterns to make the repository easier for agents to navigate and less likely to invite invented implementations.
key_learnings.speaker: Stuart
key_learnings.caveat: The guardrails were developed substantially through trial and error. The source does not establish that documentation eliminates hallucinations.

key_learnings.claim: Rivo requires a tested prompt template that supplies the task, points to analogous files, requires reading coding conventions and defines a completion checklist.
key_learnings.speaker: Stuart
key_learnings.caveat: This is a team-specific process. Stuart reports that references to similar existing code materially improve results, without a controlled comparison.

key_learnings.claim: Stuart favors uniform, reusable implementation patterns because they help the company deliver business value; his Lego-block analogy reflects a preference for constrained implementation over unnecessary novelty.
key_learnings.speaker: Stuart
key_learnings.caveat: Guest's engineering philosophy, particularly applicable to his familiar Shopify domain; not an established Adam belief.

key_learnings.claim: Rivo requires agents to provide tests, run linting and execute the test suite, while placing the final integration-test run in GitHub because it takes too long in the agent workflow.
key_learnings.speaker: Stuart
key_learnings.caveat: The linting product name is garbled in captions. Passing these checks is a process requirement, not proof of complete correctness.

key_learnings.claim: Stuart recommends winning developer support through visible results in relatively unthreatening areas such as reviews and help articles, then expanding into integrations that the team would prefer not to build manually.
key_learnings.speaker: Stuart
key_learnings.caveat: Adoption sequence is his recommendation based on Rivo's experience, not a universal sequence or an Adam implementation.

key_learnings.claim: Stuart says Shopify's changes undermined a long-running live-chat-to-review acquisition playbook, making it more attractive to improve the product and automate support instead of optimizing those review-generating interactions.
key_learnings.speaker: Stuart
key_learnings.caveat: Shopify platform changes and their scale are unverified guest assertions. His description of the old playbook as dead is an opinion.

key_learnings.claim: Rivo revisited Intercom's Fin after an initially unimpressive trial and found the later version substantially more useful, illustrating Stuart's willingness to reassess a tool as its capabilities change.
key_learnings.speaker: Stuart
key_learnings.caveat: Qualitative guest assessment; no resolution-rate, cost or satisfaction measurements are supplied.

key_learnings.claim: Rivo stores customer help articles in its repository and dispatches article-specific agent tasks that use product code as context, generate pull requests and update Intercom through an API.
key_learnings.speaker: Stuart
key_learnings.caveat: The workflow is described amid screen-sharing failures. Repository access is used to explain the product, not to intentionally publish technical internals.

key_learnings.claim: To reduce leakage of implementation details into customer documentation, Stuart explicitly instructs the agent to omit codebase technical details and says this has worked in the outputs he has observed.
key_learnings.speaker: Stuart, responding to an unidentified technical participant
key_learnings.caveat: Observed absence of leakage is not a demonstrated security guarantee. The participant raises the confidentiality concern; Stuart supplies the prompt-based response.

key_learnings.claim: After reviewing many generated help articles, Rivo began automatically merging these documentation changes, although the broader engineering workflow still describes humans as final reviewers.
key_learnings.speaker: Stuart
key_learnings.caveat: Automatic merging is described for help-document changes; it should not be generalized to all production code.

key_learnings.claim: Adam explores whether the demonstrated approach could help systematically eliminate categories of support tickets, while Rob sees an opportunity to let Tate pursue smaller engineering tasks alongside his main work.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson, likely; Rob
key_learnings.caveat: Adam's question is attributed contextually; Rob's response follows a direct address. This is a proposed application, not an achieved reduction in tickets.

key_learnings.claim: Integrations are a promising starting point when the repository contains analogous implementations: Stuart describes an agent building a Braze integration, responding to tests and evaluating Claude's review without human-written implementation code.
key_learnings.speaker: Stuart
key_learnings.caveat: One self-reported example. A human supplied the initial prompt, and earlier repository preparation remained necessary context.

key_learnings.claim: Stuart says Devin automatically produced a detailed architectural explanation of Rivo's repository, which reinforced his decision to use its code understanding to generate customer documentation.
key_learnings.speaker: Stuart
key_learnings.caveat: He praises the apparent quality, but no independent accuracy audit is reported. This capability appeared after substantial manual documentation work.

key_learnings.claim: Stuart finds a monolith advantageous for agent work because the relevant context is together, and describes Rivo's existing architecture as fortunate in that respect.
key_learnings.speaker: Stuart
key_learnings.caveat: Context-specific architectural opinion; the conversation does not compare equivalent monolithic and distributed systems.

key_learnings.claim: Stuart treats willingness to adopt AI as a condition of working together, saying he does not have time to persuade a teammate from zero; another technical participant reports a similar decision discussed with Adam.
key_learnings.speaker: Stuart; unidentified technical participant
key_learnings.caveat: The firm employment stance is Stuart's. The other participant's reference to Adam does not establish Adam's exact position or a specific personnel action.

key_learnings.claim: Adam describes this demonstration as the first systematic execution plan he has personally seen for an AI-heavy development workflow, while acknowledging that he is not an engineer.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson, likely
key_learnings.caveat: Contextual attribution. This is a statement about Adam's exposure to examples, not independent validation of the claimed 80% share.

key_learnings.claim: Stuart limits his strongest results to familiar Shopify work and junior-to-midlevel implementation tasks; his decade in a narrow domain means relatively little work is truly novel.
key_learnings.speaker: Stuart
key_learnings.caveat: This directly qualifies general claims about autonomous engineering. The technical participant explicitly distinguishes repeating an integration pattern from zero-to-one work.

key_learnings.claim: For more complex work, Stuart recommends using research-oriented AI to break the problem into smaller tasks before assigning incremental implementation to Devin.
key_learnings.speaker: Stuart
key_learnings.caveat: He mixes an account of what has worked with a proposed next stage. The transcript does not demonstrate an end-to-end novel project using this method.

key_learnings.claim: A participant argues that effective AI delegation still depends on someone who understands the code well enough to evaluate and repair it, and contrasts that with inexperienced users accepting generated products they cannot maintain.
key_learnings.speaker: Uncertain participant, possibly Rob
key_learnings.caveat: The speaker is not securely identified. Predictions that inexperienced builders' products will fail are opinions, not demonstrated outcomes or Adam's established beliefs.

key_learnings.claim: A technical participant identifies business context as an upstream bottleneck: an engineer who lacks the problem context may also be unable to provide adequate instructions to an agent.
key_learnings.speaker: Unidentified technical participant
key_learnings.caveat: This is a concern raised in a question. Stuart's latest hire was an experienced prior collaborator and CTO, so the example does not resolve onboarding for less experienced hires.

key_learnings.claim: Stuart is extending input-quality checks upstream to tickets: AI should request missing context before engineering begins, with direct routing from qualified tickets to Devin as a later step.
key_learnings.speaker: Stuart
key_learnings.caveat: This work is described as being built or planned. Fully automatic ticket-to-agent execution is explicitly a future step.

key_learnings.claim: The technical participant wants incremental wins while testing how far agents can go before extensive cleanup; Stuart recommends starting with help articles because they are less code-critical.
key_learnings.speaker: Unidentified technical participant; Stuart
key_learnings.caveat: This is a proposed rollout, not an executed result. Less code-critical does not mean customer documentation has no accuracy or confidentiality consequences.

key_learnings.claim: Stuart says Rivo moved upmarket because very small merchants are likely to churn and may not benefit enough to justify installing the product.
key_learnings.speaker: Stuart
key_learnings.caveat: The merchant revenue threshold is spoken ambiguously as under 500 thousand a year, then a million. No measured churn rate is given.

key_learnings.claim: Adam is questioning what RB2B receives in exchange for serving free users, but says those users are not materially draining resources when asked directly.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: An unresolved strategic question. He does not announce eliminating the free tier or establish that it has zero indirect value.

key_learnings.claim: Adam says user-generated content must benefit the person creating it. The Clay agency ecosystem initially helped RB2B, but its value weakened because RB2B's relevant workflow needs substantial traffic and offers fewer content possibilities around a single signal.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: Adam's retrospective explanation, not a quantified channel analysis. His comparison praises Clay's broader creative possibilities rather than rejecting agency ecosystems generally.

key_learnings.claim: Adam plans to reconnect with RB2B's customers by personally answering support tickets, talking to customers and continuing LinkedIn posts after deciding too much of his time had gone to unrelated work.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: A six-month intention stated at recording, not evidence of completed behavior or an approved mission or voice claim.

tensions_and_corrections: The title presents 80% engineering automation as current fact; Stuart initially describes moving toward 80% code generation and explains a 10/80/10 operating model. Later enthusiasm does not supply a measured company-wide percentage.
The human-final-review model has a stated exception: Stuart says help-document pull requests are now automatically merged. This exception is not evidence that all code is automatically merged.

The documentation workflow uses proprietary repository context, while Stuart relies on an instruction to prevent technical details from appearing in customer articles. His confidence and reduced review do not establish confidentiality guarantees.

Stuart reports roughly three months of broader preparation and probably one month of technical-debt reduction. Their scopes differ; the transcript does not justify choosing one as the corrected duration.

The estimated 450 versus 100 contributions imply about 4.5 times, while Stuart says 4x. The unit, period and attribution are uncertain, and the figure is not interchangeable with his separate 10x speed claim.
Successful familiar integrations are explicitly distinguished from zero-to-one development. Stuart's decade in Shopify and reusable patterns are important boundary conditions.
Stuart advocates low-friction adoption through useful demonstrations but also says unwillingness to adopt AI can make continued collaboration untenable. Both positions belong to the guest.

Stuart invested heavily in manual documentation before Devin supplied automatic architectural documentation. His historical preparation cost may not describe the same starting conditions for later adopters.
The Rivo customer-size cutoff shifts from 500 thousand a year to a million without a clear final threshold. Preserve the ambiguity instead of choosing a number.
Adam's dissatisfaction with free-tier value coexists with his statement that free users are not consuming meaningful resources. He announces no final free-tier decision.

The earlier unidentified team's four-or-five repository contributors and Adam's later three-person RB2B goal concern unclear or different scopes; they should not be reconciled into an invented headcount history.

Automatic captions vary on Devin, Rivo, the review tool, company names and personal names. The final question's apparent address to George is uncertain; the surrounding conversation identifies the principal guest as Stuart.
No fundraising history, ownership structure or bootstrapped-versus-VC conclusion is established. Lean staffing alone does not prove funding status.
Publication is August 7, 2025; the recording date is not supplied. Relative periods such as last week, three months ago and the next six months must remain relative to recording.
The guest signals sensitivity around personnel comments at 00:31:38–00:31:45. The entire extraction remains internal research, with no clearance for new public copy.
